_doc: The hostile file names every surface of filex is tested with (task #238).

ONE list: Go tests read it through package hostilenames (go:embed); the e2e specs, the web unit tests and the desktop scripts through ONE JavaScript reader, e2e/helpers/hostile-names.mjs. Never copy a name into a second list; add it here.

A name is `parts` joined: a string is itself, a number is ONE code point, {"repeat": <string or code point>, "times": n} is that many copies. Invisible, combining and emoji characters are ALWAYS written as code points, never typed: an editor shows nothing for them, and a tool that turns an escape into the character writes something nobody can review.

`refused`: no filex surface may create this name. `windows`: "invalid" when the name cannot exist as a file name on Windows. `twin`: the id of another name that is the same name to a case-insensitive or normalisation-insensitive file system (`twin_kind`: case | nfc-nfd).
`paths` are whole relative paths (a deep one) rather than names.

names.why: Turkish letters: two-byte UTF-8, and the four i's (I ı İ i) that a default case fold gets wrong
ß upper-cases to SS: a full case fold calls Straße and STRASSE one name
three-byte UTF-8 and no spaces between words: tokenisers and byte-length limits
Hangul syllables decompose into jamo under NFD: a macOS client sends a different byte string
right-to-left script with a left-to-right extension: the visual order differs from the logical one
right-to-left script with a space and a left-to-right extension
four-byte UTF-8, a surrogate pair in UTF-16: length and cutting by UTF-16 unit or byte splits it
one visible glyph made of four code points (skin tone modifier and zero-width joiner): any cut by code point splits the person
composed (NFC), the way a keyboard types it
the same name decomposed (NFD), the way macOS hands it over: different bytes, same text
a leading space is trimmed by careless parsers (FTP command lines, form fields)
Windows drops a trailing space silently, so the file it writes has another name
two spaces in a row are collapsed by HTML rendering and by some normalisers
Windows drops a trailing dot silently: report. and report become one file
a URL decoded twice turns %20 into a space
a lone % is an invalid escape: a decoder that is handed the raw name fails
decoded once too often %2F becomes a path separator
+ means a space in a query string and a form body
# starts a URL fragment: an unescaped link loses the rest of the name
? starts a query string, and Windows forbids it
; separates path parameters (some servers cut ;jsessionid) and Content-Disposition parameters
& and = split a query string; & also starts an HTML entity
an apostrophe closes a single-quoted shell, JavaScript or HTML attribute string
a double quote closes a header parameter, an HTML attribute or a JSON string, and Windows forbids it
the Windows path separator: a client or an unzip on Windows writes a folder named back
the parent folder: joined onto a path it walks out of it
only dots: Windows trims trailing dots, so on a Windows host it names the folder it sits in; the read side refuses it, so no door may create it
only dots and spaces with no .. in it: Windows trims the trailing dots and spaces, so on a Windows host it names the folder it sits in, like ... (the owner's decision for 0.57: refused)
two dots a space apart: not .., and still the folder it sits in once Windows has trimmed it
holds .. without being the parent: a guard that searches the text for .. refuses a good name
a Windows device name: opening it opens the console
a Windows device name (the printer)
a device name stays reserved with any extension and in lower case
a numbered device name with an extension
Windows forbids it, and on NTFS name:stream opens an alternate data stream
a wildcard to shells and Windows APIs, forbidden in Windows names
markup: a name written into a page unescaped runs as script; Windows forbids < and >
a shell pipe, and forbidden in Windows names
exactly 255 bytes of UTF-8 (130 characters): the most ext4, XFS and APFS hold in one name; must be accepted
one byte over the 255-byte limit of a local disk, still only 131 characters
204 characters but 404 bytes: a limit counted in characters lets it through, the disk refuses it
looks exactly like zerowidth.txt: two different files nobody can tell apart
RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE: displays as invoiceexe.pdf while the file is an .exe; the true extension must stay visible
a control character: forbidden on Windows, invisible in a listing; no door may create it
a line break inside a name breaks line-based protocols (FTP listings), logs and headers; no door may create it
no file system stores a NUL in a name; C strings end there
with case-lower: two files on Linux and S3, one file on Windows and macOS
the case twin of case-upper

paths.why: 64 folders deep, about 900 bytes: past the 260 characters of a classic Windows path, inside the 1024 bytes of an S3 key
